title: What are land acknowledgments?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain land acknowledgements: what they are, their origin in Australia's welcome to country ceremonies (starting with a 1976 Perth arts festival performance by Richard Walley), spread to Canada after the Truth and Reconciliation Commission report, and adoption in the United States. They cover how to research and write one, the criticisms (performative or "moral exhibitionism," corporate whitewashing, inaccurate history, the "noble savage" risk), the land and labor acknowledgement concept, and the land back movement including the Black Hills and a Minnesota transfer of Forest Service land to the Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe. The episode closes with a TV recommendation (Reservation Dogs) and a listener mail about pubs in Manchester and Dublin.

segments.title: Opening and what land acknowledgements are
segments.summary: Josh introduces the topic and writer Libya, describes a stadium-concert land acknowledgement as an example, and explains the purpose: to recognize that land was taken from Indigenous peoples and to prompt redress. The hosts note the practice is controversial from both the right and the left.

segments.title: Origins in Australia: welcome to country
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Indigenous welcome to country ceremony in Australia. In 1976 Maori and Cook Islander dancers would perform at a Perth International Arts Festival event only if welcomed by traditional owners, and Richard Walley, a member of the local people, performed the welcome. The practice spread through the 1980s and 1990s, and Australia's self-reflection in the 1990s boosted it.

segments.title: Acknowledgement of country and guidelines in Australia
segments.summary: The welcome to country evolved into the acknowledgement of country, a shorter speech by Indigenous or non-Indigenous speakers. The National Indigenous Australians Agency issued guidelines reserving welcome to country for Indigenous people on their own land, with non-Indigenous speakers using acknowledgement of country.

segments.title: Spread to Canada and the United States
segments.summary: Land acknowledgements took off in Canada after the Truth and Reconciliation Commission report on residential schools, during Justin Trudeau's early tenure. The practice moved to the US in the late 2010s, where a guide published by the Department of Arts and Culture (an independent group, founded by Adam Horowitz) was downloaded more than seven thousand times. Cities including Denver, Phoenix, and Portland adopted guidelines, and institutions such as the National Park Service, NASA, the Academy Awards, and the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade used them.
topics: spread of land acknowledgements in US

segments.title: What a land acknowledgement says and why people do them
segments.summary: A typical acknowledgement is given at the start of meetings, conferences, or events. It thanks past Indigenous stewards, implicitly acknowledges violence and displacement, and can point to ways to build connections. Reasons for doing them include showing solidarity with truth and reconciliation, repairing relations between American society and Indigenous cultures, and keeping the history in public view. Critics call them moral exhibitionism.

segments.title: How to research and write a land acknowledgement
segments.summary: The hosts describe steps recommended by the Native Governance Center: first examine why you are doing it, then research the Indigenous peoples of the land, which is hard because groups moved and were removed. Copying from Wikipedia or a text-message lookup service is discouraged. The best practice is to contact the Indigenous groups and work with them. Acknowledgements must be concise, and researchers may find multiple claimants to the land.

segments.title: Land and labor acknowledgement
segments.summary: Research can extend beyond land to labor. The University of Chicago's land and labor acknowledgement names four Native nations removed from the area and notes that the university was built on land donated by Stephen A. Douglas, whose fortune came from enslaved Africans. The hosts note that institutional violence is usually the focus.

segments.title: Beyond words: concrete action and the critique of corporations
segments.summary: The hosts argue an acknowledgement should be a starting point, with actions such as supporting Native causes, university tuition programs, and corporate hiring programs. They cite Graham Womack in The Atlantic, who argued land acknowledgements are counterfeit respect without time, work, or value. Corporations doing acknowledgements while doing little are open to criticism. The Real Rent Duwamish movement in Seattle is mentioned.

segments.title: Criticisms and the land back movement
segments.summary: Criticisms include the Canadian United Conservative Party halting acknowledgements in Alberta, the Montreal Canadiens acknowledgement controversy over whether the Kanien'kehà:ka (Mohawk) land claim was accurate, debates over the term stewards of the land, and the risk of romanticizing Indigenous people as the noble savage. The land back movement is discussed, including the Black Hills, where the Supreme Court found the land was taken in violation of the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868 and the Lakota refused monetary compensation. David Treuer proposed returning national park land. A Minnesota transfer of about twelve thousand acres of Forest Service land to the Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe is cited.

segments.title: Closing, TV recommendation, and listener mail
segments.summary: The hosts recommend the TV show Reservation Dogs and read a listener mail about the Marble Arch pub in Manchester and the Brazen Head in Dublin, then sign off.
